newsitem.title: THAILAND: Former Thai finmin says he quit to avoid conflict.
newsitem.headline: Former Thai finmin says he quit to avoid conflict.

text.p: Anchalee Koetsawang
Former Thai Finance Minister Bodi Chunnananda said on Tuesday he resigned from Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa's cabinet to avoid conflict with other government officials.
But Bodi, who abruptly quit on Monday, would not specify the nature of the conflict.
He also refused comment on local media speculation that he quit over a disagreement with other ministers on proposed budget cuts and the timing of new banking licence awards.
"When I accepted this portfolio five months ago, I said to myself I will do my best for the country," he told Reuters on a telephone interview.
"But now I'm in the situation where I can't continue to contribute to the country, so I'd rather leave," he said.

"I cannot go into details why I resigned. All I can say is if I had stayed on with the government, I would have had two choices -- either implement national policy the way I see appropriate or comply with others against my will."
The resignation was effective Tuesday.
Formerly chief of the Budget Bureau, the unelected Bodi was appointed finance minister in late May after Surakiart Sathirathai was forced to resign from the post.
Bodi's resignation surprised many, coming only a month before a general election that will mark the end of Banharn's administration.
Banharn dissolved parliament late last month and called a snap election.

Bodi's resignation also came less than a week after he said the government would need to cut its budget for the 1997 fiscal year, beginning October 1, because revenues were unlikely to match expenditures. The suggestion reportedly upset Banharn.
Local newspapers also speculated Bodi decided to leave after being urged to award three banking licences before the election.

The bank licence issue caused a scandal several months ago after former Justice Minister Chalerm Yoobamrung alleged that politicians were receiving kickbacks worth about 750 million baht (US$30 million) for each new licence.
The allegation was investigated by a government-appointed committee which concluded that it was groundless.

Analysts predicted Bodi's resignation would have little long-term negative impact on Thailand's ailing financial markets as he was already considered a lame-duck minister unlikely to make any policy changes before the November elections.
However, Thai stocks fell in morning trade on Tuesday on a knee-jerk reaction to the news and worries about third quarter earnings for major companies, analysts said.
Bodi said he had no plans to stay in politics or accept a cabinet portfolio in the next government.
"I just want to take a break for the time being," he said.
"I had been thinking of quitting for some time. But the decision was made on Monday," he said.

Bodi urged his successor to work toward boosting sagging exports and narrowing the country's current-account deficit, which stood at 8.1 percent of gross domestic product in 1995 and could exceed that this year, according to some economists. ($1.00=25 baht)
